extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous fiction; readers of comic travelogue and light Victorian prose
extracted.subtask_description: Comic travelogue / comic river-trip narrative exemplifying techniques for humour in first-person Victorian prose: narrator as comic persona, tall tales, physical mishap, and ironic observation. The page is a chapter of a larger humorous travel narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict truthfulness (as a comic stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I resolved, when I began to write this book, that I would be strictly truthful in all things; and so I will be, even if I have to employ hackneyed phrases for the purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the narrator’s professed commitment to 'truth' as a comic device: assert honesty while admitting (and thereby drawing attention to) conventional or hackneyed phrasing. The paradox between claiming truthfulness and deploying well-worn phrases produces humour and authorial wink. Example on page: narrator declares strict truthfulness immediately before using the familiar trope of last-minute rescue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate use of stock/trope acknowledgement (comic meta-commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Just when we had given up all hope—yes, I know that is always the time that things do happen in novels and tales; but I can’t help it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge stock narrative devices (e.g., 'just when all hope is gone') and openly confess to using them. This self-aware meta-commentary both nods to reader expectations and turns the trope into a comic element. Works as timing device to build tension then undercut it with humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and tall-tale hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Harris’s account of fighting swans escalates wildly with conflicting numbers: 'Half-an-hour afterwards they returned with eighteen other swans!... “Thirty-two,” replied Harris... “No, I didn’t,” grunted Harris; “I said twelve.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ escalating, impossible, or inconsistent details (overstated counts, prolonged battles) to produce comic absurdity. Conflicting reports from a character (changed numbers, impossible feats) emphasise unreliability and heighten comedy. Use befuddled or sleepy narrator/character voice to justify the exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating contradiction and ironic phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator's ironic statements about work: 'I like work: it fascinates me. I can sit and look at it for hours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statements that appear earnest but are undermined by a twist (contradiction or paradox) to create gentle, ironic humour. Present personal foibles as if they were virtues. Short, crisp paradoxes or reversals (claiming to love work while admitting procrastination) function as repeated comic beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-contrast comedy (old hands vs novices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated contrasts between seasoned 'old river hand' (calm, raconteur) and inexperienced younger rowers who strain away; e.g., the old man stretches out and tells marvellous feats while the novices perspire at the sculls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up oppositions between types—calm, boastful, leisurely veterans versus earnest, clumsy novices—to generate humour from mismatched expectations and behaviour. Use anecdote and caricature (the old hand's 'time-honoured lies') to characterise groups and prompt ironic commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stock tall-stories and communal ritual storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to 'the customary stretchers about the wonderful things we had done' and 'all the regular ones—the time-honoured lies that have done duty up the river'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate a repertoire of familiar, exaggerated boating anecdotes delivered as ritualistic social currency; the humour comes from the formulaic nature and the social bonding it implies. Allow a younger skeptic to mock them to expose generational differences and induce comic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic misidentification / mistaken identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends mistake a novice punter for their companion and 'peppered him with stale jokes' until they see his face and feel foolish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mistaken identity or misrecognition to create awkward social embarrassment and reversal: loud, confident mockery suddenly becomes shameful when the error is revealed. Pace the reveal for maximum comic effect and show characters' quick rationalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical mishap and slapstick as recurring device
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple scenes of physical mishap—punting mishap (man walking off the punt clinging to a pole), sculls breaking during sailing/rowing, novice rowers entangled and capsizing-like antics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ grounded, physical incidents (falls, capsizes, broken equipment) described in restrained, bemused prose to elicit laughter. Balance the vividness of the mishap with the narrator’s ironic detachment to avoid cruelty; frequently end with a rueful lesson or modest self-reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm observational moralising as ironic punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational aside: 'The sublime equanimity of the hired boatman under the ordeal affords us a beautiful lesson against ambition and uppishness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After describing a scene, deliver a calm, slightly moralising observation that reframes it—often in an unexpectedly elevated tone—so the moralising itself becomes comic. The contrast between lofty aphorism and trivial antecedent produces humour.
